extracted.intended_audience: Members and committees of Congress; congressional staff and policymakers; patent practitioners and stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining the legal doctrine, statutory and regulatory provisions, PTO practice, and proposed rulemaking concerning terminal disclaimers used to address double patenting (especially obviousness-type double patenting) in U.S. patent prosecution and their policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and effect of terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: Terminal disclaimers are a legal mechanism that allows a patent holder or applicant to relinquish part of a patent’s term, so that the patent expires earlier than it would without the disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They may be used to dedicate an invention to the public domain or strategically during patent prosecution to prevent OTDP rejections; effect is to shorten the later patent's term (often to match an earlier patent) to eliminate charges of extending monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory basis: Section 253 of the Patent Act
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 253 provides that 'any patentee or applicant may disclaim or dedicate to the public the entire term, or any terminal part of the term, of the patent granted or to be granted.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history shows terminal disclaimer provision was intended to combat double patenting by allowing later patents to expire with earlier patents; the existence and scope of terminal disclaimers ultimately derives from statute, meaning Congress can change or eliminate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory procedure: 37 C.F.R. § 1.321
rubrics_metrics.description: 37 C.F.R. § 1.321 sets forth the current procedures for making terminal disclaimers, including permitting their use to 'obviate' OTDP rejections during prosecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To make a terminal disclaimer, an applicant must state the portion of the patent term disclaimed, pay a fee, and provide that any resulting patent will be enforceable only while it is commonly owned with the earlier patent on which the OTDP rejection was based.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness-type double patenting (OTDP) doctrine
rubrics_metrics.description: OTDP (nonstatutory double patenting) prohibits acquiring a second patent on an invention that is an obvious variation on one of the inventor's earlier patents; when later claims are obvious in light of an earlier patent, the second patent is not 'patentably distinct' and is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OTDP was developed by courts to prevent evasion of statutory double patenting via slightly varied claim drafting; an OTDP rejection can be overcome via a terminal disclaimer (in contrast to statutory double patenting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between statutory double patenting and OTDP
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting (derived from Section 101) absolutely prohibits a second patent claiming the same invention; OTDP addresses obvious variants not identical inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory double patenting cannot be cured by a terminal disclaimer, whereas OTDP rejections historically can be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership condition for enforceability
rubrics_metrics.description: Any resulting patent will be enforceable only while it is commonly owned with the earlier patent on which the OTDP rejection was based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This condition is designed to ensure patents tied by a terminal disclaimer remain owned by the same entity; if ownership of one is transferred without the other, the terminally disclaimed patent becomes unenforceable under PTO rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural choices when facing OTDP rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: When an examiner rejects claims based on OTDP, the applicant can either (1) contest the OTDP rejection on its merits (e.g., argue patentable distinctness or amend claims), or (2) avoid the issue via a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a terminal disclaimer sidesteps substantive litigation with the PTO over obviousness but costs a shortened patent term; contesting the rejection may preserve term but can be more burdensome and costly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of terminal disclaimers in continuing applications (parent/child relationships)
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuing applications (continuations, CIPs, divisionals) that claim priority to an earlier application can give rise to child patents that have terminal disclaimers so they expire at the same time as the parent patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Terminal disclaimers are often used to align expiration dates among related family members and avoid OTDP rejections in the continuing-application context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical judicial justification for terminal disclaimers
rubrics_metrics.description: CCPA decisions from the 1960s held that a terminal disclaimer causing two patents to expire together is 'tantamount ... to having all the claims in one patent' and thus forecloses extension of monopoly, which justified their use to obviate OTDP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit adopted these CCPA holdings; courts have treated terminal disclaimers as a permissible cure for OTDP based on public-policy rationales about preventing extended monopoly.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO NPRM proposed enforceability condition (May 2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO proposed requiring applicants using a terminal disclaimer to agree that enforceability of any disclaimed patent depends on the validity of any patent tied to the disclaimed patent through a terminal disclaimer—if any claim of the referenced patent is held unpatentable or invalid on certain grounds by final decision, the disclaimed patent cannot be enforced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The proposal would tie the validity/enforceability of the disclaimed patent to referenced patents (including indirect ties through intermediate patents) so that patents tied by terminal disclaimers would 'stand and fall together' in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of NPRM's proposed rule (indirect ties and unidirectionality)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule would apply when a disclaimed patent is tied indirectly through 'multiple intermediate patents/applications'; it would be 'unidirectional'—the condition applies only to the disclaimed patent and not to referenced patents lacking a terminal disclaimer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: patent Z tied to Y which is tied to X would be unenforceable if a claim of X is invalidated; conversely, invalidating Z would not affect Y or X under the proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative RFC proposals (stipulation/admission of obviousness)
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO's earlier RFC proposed options like requiring applicants to stipulate that claims are not patentably distinct as a condition of filing a terminal disclaimer, or treating the terminal disclaimer as an admission of obviousness so that a family tied by disclaimers would stand or fall together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some argued these approaches conflicted with case law (e.g., SimpleAir v. Google holding a terminal disclaimer is not an admission of obviousness), raising questions about USPTO's regulatory authority to require such stipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory/legal constraint: Section 282 independent claim validity presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 282 of the Patent Act provides that 'Each claim of a patent ... shall be presumed valid independently of the validity of other claims.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opponents argue the NPRM's proposed rule departs from this principle by making a disclaimed patent unenforceable based on invalidity of a claim in a referenced patent, undermining independent assessment of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy considerations for and against changing terminal disclaimer practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Proponents argue proposed rule would promote competition, lower cost of challenging groups of patents tied by terminal disclaimers, reduce patent thickets, and improve patent quality; opponents argue USPTO may lack authority, the rule departs from independent-claim validity, will increase prosecution costs, and could harm small inventors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stakeholders (FDA, USPTO, former USPTO leaders, members of Congress) provided competing empirical and policy arguments; the comment period closed with many comments opposing the NPRM.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible Congressional responses to USPTO action
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress could disapprove USPTO's final rules under the Congressional Review Act, enact statutory amendments affecting terminal disclaimers, limit USPTO's regulatory authority, or deny funding for related activities; judicial challenges to any final rule are also possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because terminal disclaimers derive from Section 253, Congress retains leverage to change the statutory framework or otherwise respond to USPTO rulemaking.
